answers.answer: He set out from Bistritz by coach on the evening of 4 May (St George's Eve), was taken on by the Count's caleche, and reached the castle that night. His journal records the arrival in the entry dated 5 May ('5 May. The Castle.'). So he arrived on the night of 4-5 May, recorded under 5 May.

Dr John Seward. He had proposed to Lucy in May, and Van Helsing was his 'old friend and master' from before the story. Seward once sucked gangrene poison from Van Helsing's wound. On 2 September Seward wrote to Van Helsing asking him to examine Lucy.

The premise is wrong: on 30 September nothing was attacking Lucy. She had died on 20 September, and her Un-Dead body was staked and beheaded on 29 September. On 30 September the group (with the Harkers now joined) understood that a vampire had preyed on her: Count Dracula, who lived in the house next to Seward's asylum. Van Helsing told the meeting 'There are such beings as vampires', and said that had he known sooner, 'one so precious life had been spared'. Seward wrote that with the house-purchase letters earlier 'we might have saved poor Lucy'.

(1) Lucy's illness: on 2 Sept Seward decided it 'must be something mental' because her blood analysed normal. He dropped that once Van Helsing examined her and the transfusions for blood loss began. (2) Lucy being Un-Dead: on 26 Sept he rejected Van Helsing's claim and, finding her coffin empty, suggested 'a body-snatcher'. He changed his mind after seeing the white figure with the child in the churchyard, then on 27 Sept finding Lucy back in her coffin, rosier than in life ('it began to dawn upon me that I was accepting Van Helsing's theories'). The next night he saw her undead with his own eyes. (3) Renfield's sanity: on 1 Oct Seward first felt Renfield's 'reason had been restored'. He then judged the change 'yet another form or phase of his madness' and refused to release him. Renfield's dying account on 3 Oct ('I was as sane then') showed the plea had been genuine and that Renfield had let the Count in.

Fifty boxes of earth came on the Demeter via Whitby and were all delivered to the chapel at Carfax. By 1 Oct only 29 were left there, and the hunters sterilised those with Sacred Wafer. Smollet had moved six to 197 Chicksand Street, Mile End New Town, and six to Jamaica Lane, Bermondsey. Godalming and Morris destroyed all twelve on 3 Oct. Bloxam took nine to the Piccadilly house, where only eight were found and sterilised. The ninth, missing box carried the Count away on the Czarina Catherine to Galatz and then towards the castle. It was the box flung from the cart on 6 November, where the Count was destroyed.

26 July, in Mina Murray's journal at Whitby: Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep'. Lucy's mother had raised it with Mina, and Mina agreed to lock their bedroom door at night. (Lucy herself told Seward much later, on 2 Sept, that she sleepwalked as a child.)

Of Lucy's own nine records in the store, only one never mentions Arthur: her diary entry of 12 September (Van Helsing's garlic flowers, 'Good-night, everybody'). All the others name Arthur: the letters to Mina (Wednesday/9 May, 24 May, 30 Aug), the diary for 24 Aug, 25 Aug, 9 Sept and 17 Sept, and the 17 Sept memorandum ('Good-bye, dear Arthur').
5 May, in Jonathan Harker's Journal, on his first night at the castle: 'Listen to them--the children of the night. What music they make!'

experience: Exact tools helped most. `list --source lucy` printed '17 passages match (9 entries)' and, with `--without Arthur`, '8 passages match (3 entries)'. That turned Q7 into set arithmetic, though --without works per passage, not per entry: e0114 has Arthur only in part 4, so I had to read it. `grep "children of the night"` settled Q8 in one call. The search exceptions were mixed. The 'CONTINUES ... `around ID` reads the parts before and after' hint was useful: the decisive 'six boxes in each and we destroyed them all!' was in e0182.5, next to the hit. 'ERROR ARITHMETIC: The answer is computed' and 'ERROR SUPERLATIVE' refused two harmless lookups ('counted the boxes in Piccadilly... one box missing', 'last box shipped on the Czarina Catherine'). Both were false positives triggered by words like 'last' and counts, and cost me a detour to grep. SINGLE_SOURCE fired on nearly every search, including Seward's own beliefs (Q4), where one source is correct, so I learned to ignore it. In Q1 the first search returned three bare 'JONATHAN HARKER'S JOURNAL' header passages flagged OFF_QUESTION/DUPLICATES. That was fair, but the headers should not rank at all. Misleading metadata: e0081.1 is dated 1893-08-19 but the text says 'Whitby, 30 August', and e0240.1 is labelled Dr. Seward but reads like Van Helsing's memorandum ('I left Madam Mina sleeping within the Holy circle'). I wish the tool flagged when a passage's own date disagrees with its metadata date, and that `list --without` could work per entry.
